newsitem.title: USA: If it's springtime this must be Broadway gridlock.
newsitem.headline: If it's springtime this must be Broadway gridlock.

text.p: A homicidal maniac, a sinking ocean liner and Times Square hookers -- those are some of the subjects being mined for Broadway's annual flood of spring openings. And those are just the musicals.

Already the New York theatre season has been jump-started by a half-dozen recent openings, including the heralded arrival of "A Doll's House" from London and Rip Torn starring in Horton Foote's Pulitzer Prize winner, "The Young Man From Atlanta."

But in what has become an annual tradition of producers scrambling to open their shows before the deadline for the Tony Awards, no fewer than eight musicals, plays and revivals are slated to open in the next two weeks.

And there seems to be something for everyone -- revivals starring Broadway veterans Julie Harris and Stockard Channing, a political play by Pulitzer Prize winner Wendy Wasserstein with Hal Holbrook and Kate Nelligan, and musicals about the most unlikely of subjects: the bloody tale of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde and the sinking of the luxury liner Titanic.
There's even a musical about the U.S. Depression of the 1930's.

Of all the new productions, "Titanic," the $10 million musical opening on April 23, seems to be generating the most buzz, if mostly born of the sort of curiousity that met the disasterous production of the horror musical "Carrie" several seasons back. And indeed, mass death set to show tunes does seem a bit daft. But "Titanic"'s producers are philosophical.
Michael David of Dodger Productions said no thought was given to trying to gauge whether the days of the spectacular musical were waning.
"We never took this on because it presented an opportunity for scenery on the stage. It's not a musical about a helicopter or a chandelier," he told Reuters.
The show, three years in the making, received much negative publicity in its early days, largely over technical problems which have been solved.
Giving Titanic a run for its money in the off-beat department is "Jekyll and Hyde." Mind you, these shows are not folly -- their creators have proven track records.

"Jekyll and Hyde" also has the advantage of familiarity, having had a successful Houston run and a soundtrack that has been widely played. Liza Minnelli has recorded songs from the show and one was sung at President Bill Clinton's inauguration.

Other openings include "Steel Pier," by Kander and Ebb of "Cabaret" fame, which is set at a dance marathon in the Depression, and "The Life," a Cy Coleman ("Sweet Charity,") musical about Times Square prostitutes in 1980.
Fans of serious drama will have much to savor, including revivals of "The Gin Game" with Julie Harris and Lillian Hellman's "The Little Foxes" starring Stockard Channing.

The arrival of the London production of Ibsen's "A Doll's House," with Janet McTeer's daring interpretation of the classic role, caused a stir and won raves, making her a favourite for a Tony award on June 1.
